client: I just can't stop worrying about my grades after failing that important exam last semester. I keep thinking I'll lose my scholarship and disappoint everyone, and the pressure is making it hard to even focus on studying now. Part of me wonders if talking about it will help, because the problem feels so real and urgent.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying a heavy weight of worry about your future, and that pressure is making it even harder to focus when you need to most. When those thoughts about losing your scholarship come up, have you noticed any evidence that actually supports or contradicts those fears?  

What would it feel like to imagine handling this situation one small step at a time, rather than all at once?

client: I know I’ve maintained my grades so far, but it feels like it’s just a matter of time before I slip up. The pressure to keep it up is overwhelming, and when I try to study, I just freeze because I’m so scared of failing. Breaking it down into smaller steps sounds logical, but it’s hard to believe that will help when everything feels so huge and impossible.
therapist:
I hear how overwhelming this feels—like you're bracing for disaster even though you've been managing so far. That fear of slipping up seems to be taking up so much mental space that it's paralyzing you when you try to study.  

What would happen if, just for a moment, you let yourself notice that you *have* kept up your grades—what does that tell you about your ability to handle this?

client:
I know my grades are okay right now, but that just makes me more anxious—like I'm barely keeping my head above water and one wrong move will sink me. When I try to focus on the positive, it feels like I'm ignoring all the ways things could still go wrong. 

And honestly? The idea of "noticing" I'm doing okay makes me nervous—like if I let my guard down, that's when I'll actually fail.
therapist:
It sounds like even the idea of acknowledging your successes feels risky—like optimism might make you drop your guard when you feel you need to stay vigilant. That constant mental preparation for disaster must be exhausting.  

What do you think it would take to let yourself feel even a little bit of safety in this moment, without seeing it as letting your guard down?

client:
I guess I just feel like if I let myself feel safe for even a moment, something bad will happen to make me regret it. It's like I'm always waiting for the other shoe to drop. The exhaustion is real, but the fear of being caught off guard is worse. 

I don't know what it would take to feel safe—maybe some guarantee that nothing bad will happen, but life doesn't work that way. Even when things are okay, my brain keeps scanning for threats.
therapist:
It makes so much sense that you'd feel this way—your mind has learned to stay on high alert as a way to protect you, even though it's draining. That constant scanning for threats must make it hard to ever truly rest.  

What if we explored what "safety" could look like *without* guarantees—not as letting your guard down completely, but as finding small moments where the weight feels just a little lighter? Could we try that together?

client:
I get what you're saying about finding small moments of safety, but my brain keeps telling me that's dangerous. Like if I relax even a little, something bad will happen that I could have prevented. It's exhausting, but the fear feels so real. 

I don't know how to trust those small moments when my body stays tense all the time anyway. What if I try to relax and miss an actual threat? That thought alone makes my chest tighten.
therapist:
It sounds like your body and mind are locked in this cycle of tension and vigilance, even though it’s exhausting—the fear feels so immediate and real that relaxing feels almost risky. That chest tightness is a clear sign of how much this is weighing on you physically.  

What would it feel like to notice that tension—not as something to fight or ignore, but as a signal that your body is trying to protect you? Could we explore ways to gently acknowledge that protection while also letting some of the tightness ease, even just a little?

client: I get what you're saying about my body trying to protect me, but it doesn't feel helpful—it just feels like suffering. When my chest gets tight, all I can think is "here we go again" and I start panicking about when it'll stop. The idea of acknowledging the tension sounds nice in theory, but in the moment it just makes me more aware of how awful I feel.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that acknowledging the tension feels like it’s just amplifying the pain in those moments—it’s not just a concept, it’s *real* discomfort, and that “here we go again” dread is so exhausting to face over and over.  

When the panic starts to rise, what happens if you focus on just one tiny thing—like the way your breath moves, even if it’s shallow—without trying to change it or judge it? Could we try that together, very gently?

client: I get what you're saying about focusing on my breath, but when the panic hits, it feels impossible to notice anything except the overwhelming fear. Like last night, my chest got so tight I couldn't even tell if I was breathing at all. It's frustrating because these techniques sound simple, but in the moment everything just shuts down.
therapist:
I hear how frustrating and disorienting it feels when the panic takes over—like your body and mind lock down completely, even though you *want* to use these tools. That sense of everything shutting down must make it feel hopeless in those moments.  

When the fear feels that overwhelming, would it help to focus on something outside your body for a moment—like the texture of a blanket or the sound of a fan—just to give your mind one small anchor point?

client: I get what you're saying about focusing on something external, but in those moments it feels impossible to even notice anything outside my own panic. My thoughts are racing so fast that trying to focus on a blanket or sound just makes me more frustrated when I can't do it right. It's like my brain screams that nothing will help anyway.
therapist:
It sounds like the panic creates such a storm inside you that even small attempts to ground yourself feel like they're being swept away—and that frustration when it doesn’t "work" just adds another layer of distress. That hopelessness ("nothing will help") makes so much sense when you're in the thick of it.  

Would it feel any different if we didn’t frame it as "doing it right," but just as noticing what *is* happening—even if that’s only the racing thoughts themselves—without any pressure to change them?

client:
I get what you're saying about not pressuring myself to "do it right," but in the moment, it's like my brain screams that I *have* to stop the panic or something terrible will happen. Even trying to just notice my thoughts feels impossible when my chest is tight and I can't breathe.  

I guess part of me is scared that if I don't fight the panic, it'll just swallow me whole. Like noticing it means accepting it'll never stop.
therapist:
That fear of being swallowed by the panic is so understandable—it makes complete sense that you'd feel you *have* to fight it when it feels like survival. The terror that it might never stop is real in those moments, even though panic always passes.  

What if we tried something different: instead of fighting *or* accepting it, could we just name it quietly? Like, "Ah, this is the panic that feels endless right now"—not to change it, but to create even a millimeter of space between you and the storm?

client: I can see what you're saying, but naming it feels too simple when my whole body is screaming that something's wrong. When the panic hits, it's like my thoughts are racing too fast to even catch them to name them. And honestly, sometimes naming it makes me more aware of how out of control I feel, which makes it worse.
therapist:
It sounds like naming it sometimes backfires—like it highlights the chaos instead of creating distance, and that just deepens the sense of being out of control. That frustration with tools that "should" help but don’t is its own kind of pain.  

When the panic is at its worst and words feel useless, would it feel any different to try something physical—like pressing your palms together firmly, or touching something cold—not to stop the panic, but to give your body one small sensation to interrupt the cycle?
